standards.title: Guiding Principles of Risk Management for Institutions (other than Insurance Institutions) Offering Only Islamic Financial Services
standards.effective_date: absent (voluntary; supervisory authorities decide adoption, para 3)
standards.applicability: Fully-fledged banking IIFS: commercial banks, investment banks, finance houses, other fund-mobilising institutions (para 1). Excludes insurance-specific risks.
key_points: Fifteen principles across a general requirement + six risk categories: credit, equity investment, market, liquidity, rate of return, operational (paras 2, 5).
Risk management function must be independent of risk-taking, reporting to BOD or senior management outside the risk-taking unit (para 14).
Credit risk spans receivables/leases (murabahah, diminishing musharakah, ijarah) and working-capital modes (salam, istisna, mudarabah) (para 21).

Risk transformation: murabahah market risk becomes credit risk over contract life; mudarabah/musharakah capital transforms into debt on proven negligence/misconduct of mudarib/managing partner (para 22).
Default penalties: amounts cannot benefit the IIFS in most jurisdictions — disposed to charity as decided by Shariah Board (paras 22, 38).
Salam + parallel salam: no legal linkage permitted between the two contracts (para 41).

Ijarah/IMB: on permanent impairment without lessee default, IIFS must provide replacement asset or refund IMB capital portions (para 42); lessor bears asset risks, cannot charge them to lessee absent misconduct/negligence/breach (para 44).
Early-settlement discounts only by IIFS's own volition, not stated in contract (para 39).
Equity investment risk (Principle 3.1-3.3): valuation methods mutually agreed; exit strategies need Shariah Board approval (paras 61-65).

Liquidity: cashflows classed known (murabahah, ijarah, IMB, dim. musharakah) / conditional-predictable (salam, istisna) / conditional-unpredictable (open musharakah) (para 92); behavioural (not just contractual) modelling of IAH withdrawals (para 93).
Funding options named: interest-free interbank cooperation, sale-and-leaseback, central-bank arrangements on interest-free basis (para 99).

Rate-of-return risk distinct from interest-rate risk — investment results cannot be pre-determined (paras 101-103); mitigation: vary future profit ratios, new instruments, securitisation tranches (para 115).
DCR framework: IIFS may waive part/all mudarib share under market pressure — BOD-approved policy required (para 104); PER defined pre-mudarib-share, IRR post-mudarib-share IAH-only (paras 105-106).
Shariah non-compliance: transactions must be cancelled and income treated illegitimate (para 122); Shariah compliance review at least annually (para 129).
Commingled funds: formal allocation policy; reserves must not discriminate against existing IAH (para 131); separate accounts for restricted IAH (para 133).

Supervisory section paras 138-152: may set minimum liquidity per fund category (145), Shariah-compatible LOLR mechanisms (146), expected IAH return frameworks (148), audit of IAH profit allocation (152).
Qualitative standard: no percentages, risk weights or ratios anywhere.
divergence_notes: Penalty treatment varies: some jurisdictions bar any penalty except deliberate procrastination; most bar IIFS benefiting from penalties (para 22).
Non-binding promise enforceability 'varies among IIFS or from one jurisdiction to another' (para 28); in some jurisdictions a purchase order backed by promise IS binding (fn 5).
Rebate practice differs by country: rebate on subsequent transactions vs immediate discretionary rebate (para 114).

standards.title: Capital Adequacy Standard for Institutions (other than Insurance Institutions) Offering Only Islamic Financial Services
standards.applicability: Non-insurance IIFS mobilising deposits and investment accounts; extendable to self-contained windows; consolidated at IIFS holding level or individual basis (paras 6-7).
standards.reading_scope: full (reader, anchor-verified; slotting RW tables re-checked directly)
key_points: Minimum CAR not lower than 8%; Tier 2 limited to 100% of Tier 1 (para 16); denominator = credit RWA + 12.5 x (market + operational capital charges) (para 17).

Standard Formula: PSIA-funded RWA fully EXCLUDED from denominator (Appendix A(a)). Supervisory Discretion Formula: restricted PSIA excluded; (1-alpha) of unrestricted-PSIA RWA excluded; alpha portion of PER/IRR-funded RWA also deducted (Appendix A(b), para 216).

Alpha determined case-by-case by supervisors; DCR = shareholders absorbing IAH risk via smoothing; IIFS liable to IAH only on negligence/mismanagement/fraud (fiduciary, operational risk) (paras 18, 74-79).
Credit risk = Basel II standardised approach; corporates 20/50/100/150/100% by rating (para 22); short-term A-1 20%, A-2 50%, A-3/unrated 100% (para 23).
Equity in banking book (musharakah/mudarabah): simple RW 400%; 300% if withdrawable at short notice (max 5 working days); or supervisory slotting (para 29).

Slotting risk weights: Istisna specialised financing Strong 70% / Good 90% / Satisfactory 115% / Weak 250% (para 137, App B); Musharakah/Mudarabah business venture Strong 90% / Good 110% / Satisfactory 135% / Weak 270% — includes fixed +20% RW factor for NAV decline (paras 178, 190, App B-C).

CRM: hamish jiddiyah eligible only with binding promise; 'urbun; guarantees must be direct, irrevocable, unconditional; eligible collateral incl. cash, PSIA, rated sukuk (sovereign >=BB-, other >=BBB-), equities (paras 33-38).

Preferential RWs: retail/small business murabahah & ijarah 75% (<=USD250,000 per counterparty); residential real estate 35% (financing <=50% of market value); commercial RE 100% exceptionally 50% (para 42).
Past-due >90 days: 150% unsecured (provisions <20%), stepping down with provisioning (para 43).

Murabahah stages: asset on book = 15% market charge (187.5% RW); post-sale receivable = obligor RW, 100% unrated (paras 92-105). Binding MPO: acquisition cost minus collateral value minus HJ, x obligor RW (paras 94-97).

Salam: purchase-price receivable at seller RW; NO offsetting against parallel salam (paras 111-116); market risk 15% net + 3% gross simplified, or maturity ladder (para 117); where parallel salam prohibited: 15% only (para 120).

Ijarah/IMB: lease receivables for whole duration at lessee RW less asset recovery value (paras 158-160); non-binding PL asset = 187.5% RW inventory (para 163); operating ijarah residual 100% RW + 15% charge on expiry until re-leased (para 164).

Sukuk (banking book) para 193 criterion: applies only where holder owns undivided part of underlying asset with all rights/obligations; salam sukuk non-tradable, istisna and ijarah sukuk tradable; musharakah/mudarabah sukuk tradable if non-cash+receivable assets >=30% of market capitalisation (paras 193-200); sovereign sukuk carry sovereign RW (para 214).
Trading book: equities 8% specific (4% liquid diversified) + 8% general; sukuk specific risk 0-8% by rating/tenor, general via maturity method time-bands (para 45).
FX: 8% of overall net open position; gold/silver under FX per Shariah spot-equality rule (paras 47-53).
Commodities/inventory: maturity ladder 1.5% spread + 0.6% carry + 15% residual, or simplified 15% net + 3% gross; istisna WIP 8%; unbilled WIP without parallel istisna +1.6% (paras 58-62).
Operational risk: Basic Indicator 15% of average 3-year gross income; standardised 12-18% by business line at discretion; gross income excludes IAH share (paras 65-69).
Mudarabah interbank short-term placements treated as cash equivalents at mudarib counterparty RW (para 41); third-party tabarru' guarantee of capital -> guarantor RW if lower (paras 39, 185).

divergence_evidence.position: IFSB (international): classification of MPO and promise-to-lease as binding vs non-binding is left to 'the criteria and opinions set by the respective SSB of the IIFS' (para 85); PL 'may be considered as binding or as non-binding depending on the applicable Shariah interpretations' (para 150). Capital treatment differs sharply by classification.

IFSB: a binding bilateral currency promise 'is equivalent to a forward contract which is prohibited by Shariah jurists in most (but not all) countries' (footnote 13 to para 48); binding unilateral promises enter the net open FX position.

divergence_notes: Parallel salam prohibited by supervisory authority and/or SSB in some jurisdictions — different market-risk charge applies (para 120).
Salam price payable 'within two or three days as deemed permissible by its SSB' (para 108).
standards.superseded_by: IFSB-15 (IFSB-15 paras 7, 14). Kept in KB marked superseded — feeds timeline chart.

standards.title: Guiding Principles on Corporate Governance for Institutions Offering Only Islamic Financial Services (Excluding Islamic Insurance (Takaful) Institutions and Islamic Mutual Funds)
linked_standards: OECD Principles of Corporate Governance (1999, rev 2004)
standards.applicability: IIFS excluding takaful and Islamic mutual funds; commercial banks, investment banks, finance houses, fund-mobilising institutions (paras 1, 66); comply-or-explain regime (para 8).
key_points: Seven guiding principles in four parts: general governance; IAH rights; Shariah compliance; transparency of investment-account reporting (para 1).

Governance Committee mandatory recommendation: >=3 members — an Audit Committee member, a Shariah scholar (may be SSB member), a non-executive director (para 13); monitors from IAH standpoint while Audit Committee monitors from shareholders' (para 15); 'not just another Board committee' (para 17).
IAH as rabbul mal bear capital loss; IIFS as mudarib (management AND shareholders) owes fiduciary duty; IAH interests upheld no less than shareholders' (paras 22-23).
IAH monitoring right = access to information, NOT right to intervene in management (paras 24-25).
On liquidation: IAH bear loss only pro-rata to their funded assets; IIFS liable for negligence/misconduct/breach of mandate (para 32).
Smoothing concerns: PER may mask riskier investment of IAH funds (para 36); inter-generational transfer problem; undisclosed PER disposition on liquidation 'tantamount to gharar' (paras 37-38).
IRR (not PER) covers losses; IAH have no control over PER/IRR use (para 39).
IIFS shall inform IAH whenever smoothing practised, and of transfers to/from reserves (para 41); Governance Committee scrutinises PER and IRR utilisation (paras 42, 44).
Distinguish 'distribution rate' from 'profit rate' — PER smooths dividend payout, not profits earned (para 43).
Shariah mechanism must cover ex-ante and ex-post compliance incl. disposal of non-compliant income (para 48); Audit Committee ensures external auditors do ex-post Shariah reviews (para 51).
Fit-and-proper test for SSB appointment: academic qualifications, professional training, peer recognition (para 53).
IIFS shall not switch allegiance between fatawa for convenience — 'fatwa shopping' unacceptable (paras 54, 114); rulings made publicly available (para 55).
Profit-sharing ratio must be declared in advance under mudarabah, before account opening (para 62).
PER/IRR utilisation is 'an issue of public interest' — publicised in major media and annual report (para 63).
Survey findings: no IIFS lets IAH opt out of smoothing (para 98); some used PER every year for five years (para 99); no supervisor had issued smoothing rules (para 100).
divergence_notes: 'The diversity of Shariah opinions will be a permanent feature of the Islamic financial services industry' (para 45); local scholars should address local problems (para 45).
Central fatwa authorities with binding force exist in some countries — Malaysia (Islamic Banking Act 1983 s.13A; SAC), Indonesia, Sudan named (para 111 + fn 23); Jordan Banking Law Art 58(a) fn 22.
Some countries legally require IRR — Jordan Banking Law No. 28/2000 Art 55 (fn 20).
Deposit-taking may be based on wadiah or wakalah rather than mudarabah in some jurisdictions — fiduciary duties still owed (fn 12).
standards.superseded_by: IFSB-30 (IFSB-30 cover + paras 3, 5, 7). Kept in KB marked superseded — feeds timeline chart.

standards.title: Disclosures to Promote Transparency and Market Discipline for Institutions Offering Islamic Financial Services (Excluding Islamic Insurance (Takaful) Institutions and Islamic Mutual Funds)
standards.effective_date: absent (transitional phase-in suggested ~3 years for historical data, para 27 + fn 28)
standards.applicability: IIFS incl. restricted-investment-account funds managed by IIFS and Islamic windows of conventional banks with both asset and funding sides (para 5); consolidated at holding level or individual (para 6).
key_points: 17 disclosure tables across 7 sections; all on comply-or-explain basis (para 28).
Transparency framed as a Shariah obligation — Quran 4:135 and 83:1-3 cited against concealment/misrepresentation (para 2).
Frequency: semi-annual default; QUARTERLY for Tier 1, total capital, CAR components; annual for qualitative risk summaries; timely for new products (para 16).
DCR and IAH-RWA disclosures are the QUALIFYING CRITERIA for using the supervisory-discretion capital formula (para 8).
Capital structure disclosure: Tier 1 incl. shareholdings >=5% of paid-up capital, unrestricted IAH funds, PER split into shareholder and IAH components, IRR (Table 2, para 30).
IAH ratios required: PER/PSIA, IRR/PSIA, ROA, ROE, profit distributed to PSIA by type (Table 4).

Unrestricted IAH: profits earned BEFORE vs paid AFTER reserve transfers; PER/IRR movements; 3-5yr history; average declared returns by maturity (3/6/12/36-month); 6-month asset-allocation changes (Table 5).

Retail plain-language disclosures: DCR commitment is NOT contractual (would not be Shariah-compliant, fn 30); mudarib share % and waiver; withdrawal rights and penalties; PER/IRR appropriation rights; commingling; no future-performance projections (paras 42-43).
Credit risk: exposures by contract class with percentages funded by own capital/current accounts vs PSIA; penalties imposed on defaulters AND disposition of penalty monies (Table 8).
Operational risk includes Shariah non-compliance losses and fiduciary failures; disclose amount of Shariah non-compliant income (Table 12).

DCR table: 5-year history of profits before/after smoothing, PER/IRR balances, mudarib-ratio variations vs contract, benchmark comparison, analysis of alpha with supervisory rationale (Table 14, paras 62-64).
Total RWA classified by Shariah contract type (Table 15, para 66).

Shariah governance disclosures: how non-compliant earnings arise and are disposed of; whether Shariah rulings are mandatory; nature/size/number of violations in the year; zakat contributions; SSB remuneration (Table 17).
Windows: full standard applies; complete supplementary financial statements in parent's notes; window 'accounted for as a virtual branch' (paras 73-75).
Limitations acknowledged: perceived guarantees via PER/IRR reduce IAH monitoring incentives (para 96).
divergence_notes: 'Certain supervisors require IIFS to treat unrestricted IAH similarly to conventional depositors' — no loss-bearing, smoothed market-reflective return (fn 15) — direct regulator-level divergence on IAH nature.
National Shariah authority vs per-IIFS Shariah boards issuing fatawa (para 70).
standards.superseded_by: IFSB-22 (revised standard updates IFSB-4). Kept in KB marked superseded — feeds timeline chart.

standards.title: Guidance on Key Elements in the Supervisory Review Process of Institutions Offering Islamic Financial Services (Excluding Islamic Insurance (Takaful) Institutions and Islamic Mutual Funds)
standards.applicability: Authorities supervising non-insurance IIFS; risk-based supervisory approach (para 1).
key_points: Four Basel II Pillar-2 principles adapted to IIFS: internal capital assessment process; supervisory review of it; operating above minimum ratios; early intervention (para 6).
Plus a fifth concern: investor-protection issues from the IIFS role as manager of IAH funds (para 9).

Supervisor may require Standard Formula or Supervisory Discretion Formula for minimum capital (para 10); under Standard Formula IAH are investors — emphasis shifts to investor protection and firewalls, not capital (para 11).
Basel preconditions adapted: incl. a legal entity form for investment funds as alternative to mudarabah without separate legal entity (para 19(vii)).
IIFS cannot use conventional LOLR (interest-based) — contingency Shariah-compliant funding plans 'highly desirable', existing in several countries (para 22).
Additional capital above minimum must be on stated non-arbitrary basis (para 24 + fn 9); capital must cover real estate/commodity holdings outside intermediation (para 25).
Risk mitigants may require national Shariah Board approval; supervisor checks suitability, residual and operational risk (para 27).
Musharakah/mudarabah financing: slotting method guidance as alternative to simple RW (para 28).
Supervisor has discretion to impose additional operational-risk capital for Shariah non-compliance risk (para 29).

DCR treatment of IAH: supervisor judges the proportion of IAH-borne risk absorbed by IIFS capital, per-IIFS or jurisdiction-wide (para 30); where no smoothing pressure exists, IAH may be treated as restricted IAH/mutual-fund investors with mutual-fund-style controls (para 31).
Restricted investment accounts = fund management without separate legal entity — supervisor requires internal controls, risk management, disclosures to IAH (para 34).
IAH cannot enforce requirements or call for corrective action except by withdrawing funds — supervisors must protect their interests (para 44).
Related party definition includes Shariah advisors who are SSB members with product approval authority, and their family/close associates (para 41).
Home-host: host authority has primary responsibility for national Shariah-matter compliance (para 53); information sharing incl. 'validity of Shariah compliance' findings (para 55).

Windows — TWO definitions: (para 56) full window = branch/unit providing both fund management AND Shariah-compliant financing (self-contained, supervised like IIFS); (para 57) asset-side-only operations investing funds not mobilised as Islamic — different supervisory issues, risk-weighting only.
Window internal controls: competent Shariah scholar/Board expected; absence requires explanation to supervisor (paras 61-62).

Window capital calc (paras 63-64): compute CAR denominator per IFSB-2 Appendix A, compute required capital, deduct from bank's eligible capital 50% Tier 1 / 50% Tier 2; some countries segregate window regulatory capital.
Window disclosures: commingling of Islamic and conventional funds; sources covering window liquidity deficits (para 66).
Real estate investments raise risk-management and capital issues; securitised real estate = securitised restricted investment accounts, cross-sector supervision (paras 67-68).
divergence_notes: Home-host relationships must weigh 'national Shariah interpretations' among competing pressures (para 49).
Shariah regulation models vary: national Shariah Board vs systems-based requirements; prior product consent vs notification vs none (para 53).
standards.superseded_by: IFSB-16 (IFSB-16 para 6). Kept in KB marked superseded — feeds timeline chart.

standards.title: Guiding Principles on Governance for Islamic Collective Investment Schemes
standards.issued_date: 2009-01 (cover states January 2009; tracker/filename say December 2008 — cover date verified in file, line-level check)
standards.applicability: Islamic collective investment schemes meeting ALL of: pooled units/shares of equal value; established and managed per Shariah; separately financially accountable (para 6). Sukuk excluded. Excludes takaful-linked funds, pension funds, non-unitised investment accounts (para 8).
key_points: First IFSB prudential standard in Islamic capital markets (para 3); five guiding principles in four parts (para 16); five ICIS model flowcharts in appendix (para 18).
ICIS usually structured under mudarabah or wakalah investment (fn 8).
Governing body must protect independence of each governance organ; 'Chinese walls' established and strictly adhered to (para 20).
Unethical practices named: front running, insider dealing, warehousing, rat trading, dustbin (fn 20).
Outsourced governance functions reviewed at least every six months (para 25).
Whistle-blowers may escalate to supervisory authorities without employment consequences (para 26).
Prospectus: 10 mandated disclosure items incl. SSB identity, terms of reference, qualifications, other associations AND their fees; mechanics of smoothing returns (para 35).
Off-balance-sheet restricted investment accounts must not escape fund-level disclosure/scrutiny (para 37).

Shariah governance: ex-ante fatwa organ + compliance officer; ex-post internal Shariah audit (quarterly/semi-annual/annual) + external verification by SSB, independent Shariah firm, or external auditor with expanded terms (para 42).
Portfolio screening before unit issuance and periodically after changes; internal screening needed beyond Islamic indexes for non-securitised portfolios (paras 46-48).

Purification (tanqiyyah): income tainted by impermissible or shub'hah sources removed before distribution — incl. equities crossing Shariah boundaries after mergers; recipient charities must not be related to any ICIS insider (paras 49-50).
Related-party transactions: at least arm's-length, GB + SSB approved, disclosed at least in annual report (para 54).
Valuation: valuer functionally separate from fund management; divestment to sponsor/manager requires INDEPENDENT valuer (paras 55-56); valuation system reviewed at least annually (para 57).
Smoothing via PER/IRR (or reduced mudarib share/wakil fees) risks false performance impressions; independent governance organ scrutinises use (paras 59-61, 66).
Performance fees must not incentivise excessive risk nor breach equality between investors; disclose timeframe, independent benchmark, formula; fee caps as % of NAV encouraged (paras 63-65).
divergence_notes: SSB formation requirements vary: some supervisors dictate, most leave to market forces (para 44).
SPV insolvency non-recognition in some countries pushes ICIS establishment to Bahamas/Cayman/BVI (fn 15).

standards.title: Capital Adequacy Requirements for Sukuk, Securitisations and Real Estate Investment
standards.applicability: Non-insurance IIFS; extendable to self-contained windows; risk-weight methodology usable for sukuk/real-estate held by non-self-contained windows (para 2).
key_points: Three sukuk structures (para 10): (a) asset-backed (holders bear asset losses — the IFSB-2 category); (b) asset-based with repurchase undertaking / binding promise by originator ('pay-through' — credit risk is the ORIGINATOR's); (c) pass-through asset-based (issuer guarantees, credit risk = issuer's rating). Standard covers (b) and (c).
Where repurchase undertaking exists, holder RW = originator's credit RW, subject to any Shariah-compliant enhancement by issuer (para 13).
Sukuk funds must go to specified assets; certificate = proportionate ownership transferred for a fixed period to holders (para 8).

Tradability: financial-asset sukuk (murabahah/salam receivables) non-tradable; tradable when pooled with non-financial assets above a minimum ratio per Shariah rules (paras 26-27); musharakah/mudarabah venture sukuk tradable, unrated held-to-maturity gets IFSB-2 equity-position treatment (para 28).

Derecognition criteria (para 29): substantially all risk transferred; no effective/indirect control by transferor; holders have claim ONLY on asset pool (so non-ABS structures NEVER qualify); transferee is SPE with pledgeable interests; clean-up calls only at <=10% remaining consideration.

True sale — four Shariah criteria (para 32): no recharacterisation as secured loan; originator bankruptcy cannot affect transferred assets; transfer perfectible at issuer's election; free of prior liens.
Retained securitisation exposure RWs for originator: AAA to AA- 20% / A+ to A- 50% / BBB+ to BB- 100% / B+ and below 150% / unrated 100% (para 41).
Implicit support restricts derecognition; cannot come from IAH funds without consent (= misconduct); must be publicly disclosed with capital impact (para 42).
Liquidity facilities: 20% CCF (<1yr), 50% CCF (>1yr), 100% CCF if externally rated (para 43); servicer cash advance (qard-based) may get 0% RW at national discretion (para 44).
Credit enhancement by structure — Basel II para 567 scale: 20/50/100/350%/deduction/deduction; deductions 50% Tier 1 + 50% Tier 2 (paras 49-50).
Originator's retained equity first-loss position (e.g. 10% of ijarah pool, income waiver via hibah): deduction from capital or 1250% RW (para 48).
Real estate: investment vs financing distinguished by existence of regular customer cash flow (para 55); three investment categories incl. holdings past ~6 months without binding promise (para 56).
Real estate investment RW: 187.5% (15% capital charge) for single investment exposure and non-binding-stage holdings; operating ijarah per IFSB-2 para 166 (para 69, App 2).

Concentration limits recommended: aggregate 60% of regulatory capital, single 15%; alternative split limits incl. 15% of UIAH funds (para 65); restricted accounts: no aggregate limit proposed (para 67).
Real estate subsidiary investment: deduct carrying amount if >15% of capital base (para 62).
Appendix 1: sukuk vs bonds vs shares comparison table (ownership vs debt; not guaranteed by issuer; Shariah-compliant purposes only).

divergence_evidence.position: IFSB: asset-based sukuk rest on a repurchase undertaking (binding promise) by the originator — treated as prudential fact shifting credit risk to originator (paras 10(b), 13, 16); enforceability/strength of the undertaking in the jurisdiction is flagged as a risk (para 16).

divergence_notes: Scholars differ on separating legal and equitable title — impedes securitisation in unperfected transfer structures (fn 11 to para 32).
Rahn is possessory in certain jurisdictions, making perfection difficult (para 15(a)).
standards.superseded_by: IFSB-15 (IFSB-15 paras 7, 14). Kept in KB marked superseded — feeds timeline chart.

standards.title: Guiding Principles on Governance for Takaful (Islamic Insurance) Undertakings
standards.applicability: All takaful undertakings irrespective of legal status and operational model (para 9); limited applicability to retakaful (para 10); comply-or-explain disclosures (para 12).
key_points: Six guiding principles in three parts (para 7).

Takaful undertaking = two-tier hybrid: mutual (participants' funds) + commercial company (the takaful operator, TO) (para 5); pure mutuals rare — not recognised in some legal systems, capital adequacy hard (fn 4).

Three main models (para 13): mudarabah (TO = mudarib, share of investment profit and/or underwriting surplus); wakalah (pre-agreed fee % of contributions covering management, distribution, operational margin; optional performance fee); wakalah-mudarabah hybrid (wakalah for underwriting, mudarabah for investment).
Underwriting fund belongs to participants, not shareholders; risk shared among participants, not transferred to TO (paras 15, 19).
Family takaful: contributions segregated into PIF (investment) and PRF (risk, tabarru' basis); segregation percentages part of product design, cannot be unilaterally altered (para 16).

TO is 'not the owner but only the custodian' of the takaful fund; not liable for deficit/loss absent misconduct/negligence — yet has wide discretion with no participant control mechanism (para 20); participants excluded from general-meeting voting (para 22).
Shareholders bear no fund deficit except providing qard facility to a deficient PRF; TO capital exposed where qard unrecoverable over any reasonable period (para 19(iii)).
Each TO shall appoint an actuary reporting to BOD: risk monitoring, liability/solvency investigation, contribution levels, PRF asset valuation (para 47).

Governance Committee: >=3 members — independent NED, Shariah scholar (may be SSB), actuary; optional participants' representative (para 49); scrutinises costs charged to funds and surplus levels 'especially where the TO receives a percentage share of the surplus as a fee' (para 53).

Disclosure: qard facility availability and conditions (para 55); annual audited statements state TO position on back-up qard capital (para 66); takaful model disclosure incl. remuneration split by Family/General, surplus distribution and ratios (para 69); mudarabah PSR declared in advance at point of contract (para 72).
Family takaful investment products are defined-contribution, never defined-benefit (para 56); PRF/PIF assets and takaful/shareholder funds clearly separated (para 57).

Solvency: TO 'walking away' from PRF insolvency is 'simply unacceptable... No supervisory authority should permit this' (para 82); qard regimes part of licensing in some jurisdictions; Governance Committee + supervisor involved before qard terms finalised (para 83).
TO policy list must fix: surplus ratio/weightings by line, qard conditions, cross-PRF offsetting, participant calls to cover deficits, surplus entitlement periods (para 86).
Deficiency due to misconduct and negligence borne by shareholders (para 88).
Retakaful: prefer retakaful operators over conventional reinsurers (para 91); investment strategies of shareholder and takaful funds kept separate; purification of tainted returns (paras 92-94, 102).
divergence_notes: IDB Shariah Committee rejects TO taking any percentage of underwriting surplus — 'an underwriting surplus is not a profit' (fn 7 to para 13; also fn 15) — while the mudarabah surplus-sharing model is in live use in some operations.
Separate regulation of takaful vs shareholder funds exists in some jurisdictions, not in many others (para 92).

standards.title: Guiding Principles on Conduct of Business for Institutions Offering Islamic Financial Services
linked_standards: IOSCO International Conduct of Business Principles
standards.applicability: ALL IIFS across banking, takaful and capital-market segments, including windows, Islamic insurance, Islamic mutual funds and fund management companies (para 3 + acronyms).
key_points: Seven principles: truthfulness/honesty/fairness; due care and diligence; capabilities; information about clients; information to clients; conflicts of interest and duty; Shariah compliance.
Ethical conduct is a Shariah obligation, sometimes required for contract validity; binds all staff 'irrespective of their religious beliefs' — especially relevant for windows (para 6).

Misleading information about Shariah compliance of products or SUKUK issuances = named misconduct (para 12); manipulating the Shariah approval process by non-disclosure to scholars unacceptable (paras 17-18).
Wa'd: 'Shariah considers a unilateral promise as an undertaking that is ethically and in some cases legally binding'; promising without serious intent unacceptable (para 19).
Two classes owed due care: shareholders AND IAH/takaful participants — unlike conventional single-class duty (para 21).

Financing conduct: lax creditworthiness checks relying on collateral unacceptable where enforcement inflicts hardship; assist non-culpable distressed debtors (restructure) before enforcing collateral (paras 23, 25).
Sukuk due diligence: holders of sukuk later found non-compliant may have to dispose at loss and donate profits to charity (para 26).
'Caveat emptor' NOT applicable without qualification — seller absolved only after exhausting all transparency about known defects (para 38).
Murabahah validity requires disclosing original cost INCLUDING discounts received, plus mark-up (para 39).

No small print, no hidden costs; commissions fully disclosed; recommendations driven by client benefit not commission (para 40); no hard selling; cooling-off periods, e.g. two weeks for family takaful savings (paras 41, 44).

Illustration 10 numerics: unrestricted mudarabah account with up to 25% of profit to PER, up to further 20% of IAH share to IRR, 20% of placement treated as current account — all must be fully explained to customer (para 45).
Gharamah (late-payment penalty) must be spelled out in contract and flagged before signature (para 46).
Conflicts: link management pay to UIAH returns as mitigation (para 52); family takaful operator duty to PIF participants must not be subordinated to shareholder value (para 53).
Shariah compliance 'paramount': competent Shariah compliance officers with authority; ex-ante and ex-post mechanisms (paras 54-55).
UIAH must be told mudarib/wakil cannot guarantee against capital impairment (para 58); family takaful operator cannot offer defined-benefit pension product (para 59).
divergence_notes: 'The Shariah compliance of certain sukuk structures is a matter of disagreement, but in general a majority opinion may be identified' (para 26); disputed features listed fn 9: originator repurchase at pre-agreed price; mudarib interest-free loan topping returns to benchmark; tranched senior/subordinated structures.
Self-assessment questionnaire asks whether product's validating opinion 'represents the mainstream view of scholars internationally' (App 2 Q1.2.1).

standards.title: Guiding Principles on Shariah Governance Systems for Institutions Offering Islamic Financial Services
standards.star_overlap: IFSB-10 was already clause-verified in standards_kb_star.json (prior session). This entry is the enriched full-read version. BV: load ONLY ONE IFSB-10 entry — either merge these additions into star.json's entry or let this one supersede it. Do not double-load.
standards.applicability: IIFS incl. windows, takaful institutions, Islamic mutual funds, fund management companies (acronyms + definitions); proportionality by size/complexity (Principle 1.1); comply-or-explain (para 9).
key_points: Nine guiding principles in five parts: general approach; competence; independence; confidentiality; consistency (para 7).

Shariah governance system = institutional arrangements for independent oversight over four processes: pronouncement issuance; dissemination via ISCU; internal Shariah compliance review/audit; annual Shariah review/audit (para 3).
A pronouncement once implemented becomes hukm shar'i binding the IIFS with full legal effect (para 3(a)).
Fatwa due process: rigorous board deliberation + detailed scrutiny of legal contracts and documents (para 3(a)).
Where a central authority exists, the IIFS-level board does not contradict it (para 3(a) + fn 7).
ISRU reports to the Shariah board (unlike internal audit reporting to Audit Committee); ISCU sits in compliance, separate and independent from business units (para 3(b)-(c)).

Recommended board composition: at least three members, possibly trained in different schools of jurisprudence, mixed experience and nationalities; commerce/finance exposure (para 17); single-scholar arrangements sacrifice collective wisdom, raise independence doubts (fn 13).
Some authorities cap number of boards a national-panel member may serve; some prohibit national panel members sitting on market players' boards (para 13).

Fit-and-proper: good character + competence limbs; applies to Shariah board AND ISCU/ISRU officers (paras 26-30); minimum academic bar: bachelor/ijazah in Shariah sciences incl. fiqh al-muamalat, strong usul al-fiqh, good Arabic (App 4).
Chairman: >=3 years' pronouncement experience or >=4 years post-qualification teaching/research (App 4 item 2).

Independence disqualifiers: current/recent full-time employment at IIFS, immediate family in senior management, compensation beyond board fees, >=5% stake with significant IIFS payments (para 42); 'significant' guided at 20%+ above normal fee rate (fn 24).
Formal performance assessment of board and each member; outcomes incl. seeking resignation (paras 36-39).
Information rights: complete/adequate/timely information before all meetings; independent access to senior management, ISCU, ISRU; professional advice at IIFS expense (paras 46-50).
Confidentiality: seven categories of confidential information; duties survive tenure; non-disclosure agreement per member (paras 52-55).
Consistency: consensus first, simple majority only after reasonable time; member opinions consistent across the boards they serve (para 57); dissents recorded in minutes (App 2 item 10).
Board-BOD dispute route: on record to shareholders/supervisor, supervisor informed before public announcement; whistle-blower access to shareholders (para 22 fn 17, para 40).

Meetings with BOD at least twice a year; non-Shariah professionals on board do not vote on Shariah matters (App 2 items 5-6); duties include overseeing zakat computation and distribution (App 1 item 4(iv)).
Fallback hierarchy where no central authority: follow internationally recognised bodies' pronouncements, else document and publish own for open assessment (para 60).
divergence_notes: Jurisdiction models diverge: market-led vs mandated systems (para 11); centralised national boards vs IIFS-level boards (para 13).
Members possibly trained in different schools of jurisprudence; ethics require appreciating diversity of opinions among schools of thought (para 17; App 3 item 3(iv)).

standards.title: Standard on Solvency Requirements for Takaful (Islamic Insurance) Undertakings
standards.applicability: All takaful and retakaful undertakings; extendable to takaful windows at supervisory discretion (para 5); single-entity focus, no group supervision (para 6).
key_points: Seven Key Features (KF1-KF7), principles-based: 'does not prescribe specified quantitative techniques' (para 2).
Total balance sheet approach WITH clear separation of PRF and shareholders' funds (KF1); two-level structure: PRF solvency + TO capital for own obligations incl. qard backing (para 28).

Solvency emphasis on PRF; PIF normally excluded — investment risk fully borne by participants, no qard backing needed; but PIF liquidity for withdrawals must be managed, qard possible if PIF assets illiquid (paras 7, 70).
Benchmark criterion: meet liabilities with defined probability, e.g. 99.5% over 1 year (paras 8, 60); standard model or supervisor-approved internal models (paras 60, 64).

PRF requirement: assets = technical provisions (best estimate + risk margin, market-consistent, portfolio-transfer benchmark, para 26) + solvency margin reserves; may include standby qard-basis facility (para 30.A).

Qard facility: earmarked shareholders' assets count toward PRF capital 'if local regulation permits' (paras 14-15); NOT the sole permissible mechanism, no amount prescribed (para 16); investment income of undrawn facility stays with shareholders (para 34).

TO must hold unencumbered capital beyond own solvency needs for any earmarked qard amount (para 17); right to repayment of drawn qard is NOT an asset for TO solvency; no double counting (paras 31, 35, 41).

Winding-up priority is decisive: qard pari passu with participants' claims = partial capital quality; participants ranking ABOVE qard = full regulatory capital (para 18); priority must be clear in insolvency law and disclosed (para 53).

Qard acceptance conditions (para 51): facility non-withdrawable until PRF meets solvency independently; TO consents that in winding-up drawn qard is treated as DONATED to the PRF as needed for participants' claims.

Control levels: MCR + PCR per PRF; MTC + PTC for shareholders' fund (para 43); MCR breach without acceptable restoration plan = prohibited from writing further business (para 44); supervisor may force immediate qard draw-down, trigger not below technical provisions (paras 46-47).

Ring-fencing: default assumption = NO transferability between funds absent clear legal/contractual framework — generally raises total capital (para 40); no mixing Family and General business in one PRF unless Family is short-term (para 38).
Risk formulae (para 62): PRF: SR = RCPR + RCUR + RCCR + RCMR + RCOR; TO: CR = RCCR + RCMR + RCOR; correlation/diversification allowed; liquidity risk excluded from formula.

Risk mapping (para 61): PRF credit risk incl. contributions receivable, retakaful recoveries; market risk incl. salam commodities, sukuk, murabahah assets, ijarah assets, FX; operational risk incl. Shariah non-compliance, purification of tainted income, fiduciary risk; non-recovery of drawn qard = credit risk on earmarked shareholder portion (fn 32).
Real estate permissible but risky — supervisor may impose type/level/concentration limits or charges; less problematic for Family long-term savings (para 67).

ORSA-style review: TO conducts own risk and solvency assessment separately for PRF(s) and shareholders' fund (para 69); TO should make each PRF self-sustaining over time so qard facility becomes superfluous (paras 33-34).
Public disclosure of qualitative and quantitative solvency information; risk overview in annual report (para 73).
divergence_notes: IDB Shariah Committee disagrees with TO taking percentage of underwriting surplus — 'not a profit' (fn 8 to para 9).
Qard priority in winding-up diverges by jurisdictional regulation (para 18).
Window issue: whether non-Shariah-compliant TO assets can back a qard to the PRF (fn 4).
standards.superseded_by: IFSB-28 (IFSB-28 para 3). Kept in KB marked superseded — feeds timeline chart.

standards.title: Guiding Principles on Liquidity Risk Management for Institutions Offering Islamic Financial Services [Excluding Islamic Insurance (Takaful) Institutions and Islamic Collective Investment Schemes]
standards.applicability: Banking IIFS: full-fledged Islamic banks, Islamic investment banks, Islamic subsidiaries, windows, other fund-mobilisers; proportionality (para 5). Excludes takaful and ICIS.
key_points: 23 guiding principles: 15 for IIFS, 8 for supervisory authorities (para 4; sections 3.1-4.8).

Structural constraint: no interest-based interbank borrowing; in most jurisdictions debt transferable only at FACE VALUE — forces higher cash/non-earning liquid holdings than conventional banks (para 20).
Liquidity infrastructure = 13 jurisdiction-level elements incl. Islamic money market, Shariah-compliant monetary instruments, safety net, insolvency framework, Islamic benchmarks (paras 21-22).

CMT dual-use warning: distinguish short-term interbank CMT from longer-term CMT deposits/financing; disproportionate use 'may aggravate liquidity risk and expose the IIFS to excessive leveraging' (para 27); supervisors intervene on heavy long-term CMT reliance (para 130).
Current accounts are qard-based (wadiah yad dhamanah legally equivalent in some jurisdictions, fn 25) — repayable in full on demand (para 46).

UIAH runs: contractually loss-bearing, but panic withdrawals on rate-of-return, Shariah non-compliance or reputational events; early withdrawal requires profit waiver via mubara'at; rate-of-return risk -> withdrawal risk -> 'can transform into a systemic liquidity crisis' (para 48).
Smoothing/DCR link: GN-3 techniques factored into liquidity analysis; only IRR may cover UIAH investment losses (para 57 + fn 27).

Murabahah-account/CMT funding renewal risk: Shariah requires terminating the initial contract before renewal — stressed counterparties simply don't renew; some Islamic investment banks failed in the crisis on CMT renewal risk (para 51 + fn 38).
Interbank market mostly unsecured mudarabah/CMT/wakalah; shortage of Shariah-compliant repo alternatives (paras 54, 101).

Per-contract liquidity risks catalogued: murabahah cancellations and late payment; ijarah re-lease/sale failure; salam illiquid commodities + no pre-delivery exit; mudarabah/musharakah unpredictable cashflows (para 58); cash-flow taxonomy known/conditional-predictable/conditional-unpredictable (para 62).
IIFS normally do not actively manage net funding requirement beyond six to eight weeks (para 64).

Liquidity buffer: cash + unencumbered Shariah-compliant HQLA; calibrated to severe stress 1-2 weeks, less severe 2-4 weeks, persistent beyond (paras 87-89); sukuk HQLA features listed incl. not-financial-institution obligation, multilateral/high-rated sovereign issuers (fn 48).
Contingency funding plan: 6 components, 3 crisis stages, annual review (paras 93-99); constraints: hard to sell sukuk, scarce compliant collateral, minimal securitisation (para 100).
FX liquidity: limit exposure in illiquid/low-convertibility currencies; compliant FX-swap alternatives scarce (paras 112-116 + fn 66).

LOLR: where available, via mudarabah, CMT, sale/buy-back of eligible collateral (mostly government sukuk), qard; unavailable or undefined in many jurisdictions (para 138); expand eligible collateral to PSE/corporate/multilateral/foreign-sovereign sukuk, future IILM sukuk (para 140 + fn 72).
Islamic investment banks mostly ineligible for LOLR — supervisors should consider extending support (paras 86, 141, 144).
Government sukuk serve 5 roles; supervisors should press for regular issuance programmes, Shariah-compliant deposit insurance, market makers (paras 161-163).
Appendix metrics adapted from Basel III common metrics: maturity mismatch bands, significant counterparty >1% balance sheet, significant currency >=5% liabilities (Appendix).

divergence_evidence.position: IFSB: 'in most jurisdictions it is not allowed to transfer its debt, other than at its face value' (para 20); murabahah portfolios 'cannot be resold in the market due to Shariah restrictions on the selling of debt' (para 56); Shariah rulings on permissible securitisation structures 'may vary between jurisdictions' (fn 39). Direct prudential consequence: structural liquidity disadvantage of IIFS.

IFSB: CMT treated as prudential fact with explicit overuse warnings — excessive leveraging risk (para 27), supervisory intervention on heavy long-term reliance (para 130), renewal risk documented as crisis failure cause (fn 38). No permissibility ruling made.

divergence_notes: 'Slow progress and disagreements regarding Shariah opinion on the possible alternatives to a repurchase agreement' keep repo reliance low (para 101).
Home-host divergence on acceptability of various sukuk from a Shariah perspective (para 152).
Window placements of excess funds with conventional head office raise Shariah issues on profit payment (para 85).

standards.title: Guiding Principles on Stress Testing for Institutions Offering Islamic Financial Services [Excluding Islamic Insurance (Takaful) Institutions and Islamic Collective Investment Schemes]
standards.effective_date: 2013-01 (members expected to apply by January 2013, para 16)
standards.applicability: Full-fledged banking IIFS with proportionality; extendable to self-contained windows (para 11); consolidated or individual basis (para 12).
key_points: 29 guiding principles: 22 for IIFS, 7 for supervisory authorities (para 10).
IIFS resisted crisis first-round effects (no speculative derivatives/toxic CDOs/excess leverage) but hit by second-round effects, e.g. real estate via IMB (para 5 + fn 2-3).
'Market risk in the banking book' is an IIFS specificity: market and credit risk arise together; murabahah market risk transforms into credit risk after sale (para 7).
2010 survey (131 responses, 15 jurisdictions): reverse stress testing rarely used; DCR/IAH/real-estate/Shariah non-compliance get only 'some consideration'; disclosure 'very weak' (para 15).
BOD ultimately responsible; must challenge model assumptions and scenario selection (para 28).

Governance Committee actively involved in unrestricted-PSIA scenarios (commingled funds, IIFS as mudarib) (para 30); collaboration framework between risk management, SSB and Governance Committee required (para 39).

IIFS-specific stress factors: sukuk/real-estate credit risk; equity/sukuk/real-estate/FX market risk; mudarabah/musharakah investment risk; rate-of-return risk; DCR; Shariah non-compliance operational risk (para 49).
Rate-of-return risk mechanics: sale-based returns fixed by Shariah while benchmarks move; leads to DCR (para 51 + fn 26).
PSIA scenarios must assess: DCR extent via alpha; likelihood of repaying UIAH principal in distress; withdrawal risk; PER/IRR sufficiency; deposit-insurance/guarantee schemes (para 74).
Smoothing vs loss-covering: covering losses is NOT Shariah-compliant unless via IRR or donation without contract (hibah) (para 75).

Capital stress: hypothetical supervisory rise in alpha; 'stressed alpha' from stressed-period data; alpha ranges 0-1 per GN-4 (para 79); must show capital above regulatory minimum through a reasonably severe recession (paras 81-82).
Credit stress: recovery restrictions under Shariah contracts (para 84); no credit swaps/options/derivatives available — challenge effectiveness of compliant mitigation (para 89).
Sukuk stress list: embedded triggers, tranching subordination, ratings migration, refinancing/restructuring, Shariah-contract vs civil-law legal risk (para 93).
CMT: no rollover unless initial contract terminated (fn 42); 'crowded trades' market impact; stress ex-ante caps on intraday gross turnover / net outstanding CMT (paras 101-102).
Liquidity stress: cash-flow ladder by contract class; murabahah receivables unsellable (paras 105-109).

Shariah non-compliance stress: income forfeiture to charity, contract invalidation with high rewinding cost, withdrawal crisis, compensation, court costs (paras 111-114); outputs discussed with SSB (para 115).
Reverse stress testing from known failure outcome; no capital add-on expected (paras 126-129).
Frequency: market-sensitive daily/weekly; murabahah receivables/ijarah monthly/quarterly; ad-hoc on deterioration (paras 134-136); methodology review at least annually (para 130).

Supervisors: system-wide common-scenario and macro tests complement (not substitute) internal tests (paras 163-167); corrective tools incl. capital above Pillar 1 minimum (para 173); common reporting format for benchmarking (paras 179-180).

divergence_evidence.position: IFSB: stress testing must contemplate a future ruling of NON-permissibility on products in use — worked example: 'if an IIFS were dependent on CMT for deposits and these transactions were subsequently to be considered non-permissible, what would be the resulting liquidity stress?' (fn 49 to para 112). Divergent fatawa across jurisdictions listed as a stress risk factor (para 113(e)).

divergence_notes: 'The Shariah compliance of certain structures is a matter of controversy' (para 112); scholars may rule products already in use non-compliant (paras 111, 113(d)).
Judicial precedents non-binding in certain jurisdictions amplify legal uncertainty at the Shariah-contract/civil-law interface (para 93(k)).

standards.title: Standard on Risk Management for Takaful (Islamic Insurance) Undertakings
linked_standards: IAIS ICPs (2011) esp. ICP 8 and ICP 16
standards.applicability: All takaful undertakings under Family, General or Composite licences; adaptable to retakaful, takaful windows, other Islamic insurance forms (para 8); individual-entity focus, extendable group-wide (para 9); principles-based, no quantitative standards (para 5).
key_points: Organised as lettered sections (no numbered key principles): risks; enterprise risk management; supervisory review; systemic risk (TOC).
TU-specific risks: Shariah non-compliance risk, fund-segregation risks, retakaful risks (para 18).

Shariah non-compliance risk 'is unique to TUs' among insurers: may invalidate contracts, strip participant protection, cause loss/reputational damage/regulatory action (para 19); arises in product development and investment (paras 21-22); classed as operational risk with prevent/detect/correct controls incl. divestment of assets turning non-compliant (para 34(x)).
Fund segregation creates agency risks absent in proprietary insurers; loss of diversification between funds raises economic capital needs (paras 23-24).

Qard mechanics: SHF risk = qard being required AND not repaid (para 25); qard committed to PRF is SHF credit risk, most likely at business commencement/growth (new business strain) or after major losses (para 37(v)); PRF deficiency repayable only from FUTURE SURPLUSES — adverse selection (non-renewal) and intergenerational inequity follow (para 35(vi)).
Expense misattribution risk: Shariah requires funds not be commingled; expense allocation vs TO fee needs governance + Shariah approval, set out in contracts and marketing (para 34(xi)-(xii)).
SHF expense risk: fees from PRF/PIF may not cover TO's committed expenses; over-optimistic assumptions cause SHF loss (paras 27, 35(iv)).

Underwriting management risk (PRF mismanagement) is a TO/SHF risk, not a PRF risk (para 34(iii)); TO may have LESS appetite for underwriting volatility than a conventional insurer due to lapsation risk (para 35(v)).

PRE (participants' reasonable expectations) = the standard's DCR analogue: TO representations may oblige the TU to meet return/surplus expectations 'notwithstanding that no actual guarantee has been provided'; feeds capital position, product design, pricing, actuarial advice, Shariah review (para 35(xii)). Term DCR itself absent.

Retakaful: recoveries rest on tabarru' — shortfall risk 'qualitatively different from credit risk' but managed similarly (para 37(ii)); risk-sharing retakaful requires due diligence on provider's risk selection and pool status (para 30).

Liquidity: PRF/PIF issues can arise from wakalah-fee timing or surplus-distribution policy (para 38(ii)); qard draw-down may need supervisory approval (para 38(iii)); liquidity support FROM PRF/PIF TO the SHF prohibited (para 38(iv)).

ERM: risk appetite set separately per fund (para 48); nine-item minimum risk register (para 55); three lines of defence + four control functions + Shariah board as governance function (paras 68-69); CEO/Chief Actuary should not normally be CRO (fn 22).

Shariah board consulted on all matters with significant non-compliance risk; receives risk-register extracts, assessments, incident reports (paras 74, 77); internal audit designs Shariah-compliance testing programme for Shariah board approval (para 83(ii)).

ORSA required whether or not regulation demands it (para 84); must respect fund separation so stresses are not masked cross-fund; model qard availability and repayment (para 86); stress + reverse stress testing; 1-year horizons common (para 93).
Disclosure: per fund and per risk category — nature, exposure, management effectiveness opinion (para 98).
Systemic: dominant retakaful operator may be systemically important (paras 107-108); concentration in the limited Shariah-compliant investment universe is a systemic exposure (para 109).
divergence_notes: 'What may be deemed permissible by one scholar or in one jurisdiction may be considered otherwise by a different scholar or in another jurisdiction' (para 20); national law may even compel non-compliance, e.g. holding riba-bearing government debt (fn 9).
Differing views on validity of conventional reinsurance for takaful; darurah (necessity) conditions judged differently by different authorities (para 29 + fn 13; para 102(vii)).
Waqf model changes the nature of fund ownership (fn 6).
